items.zh: 復次，即前所說自性乃至業等五事，當知皆由三處所攝。
items.en: Further, one should understand that these five things previously discussed — self-nature, and so on up through activity — are all comprised within three categories.

items.zh: 謂由色聚故，心心所品故，及無為故。
items.en: Namely: the category of matter aggregates, the category of mind and mental factors, and the category of unconditioned dharmas.

items.zh: 除餘假有法。今當先說色聚諸法。
items.en: This excludes all other conceptually existent dharmas.

items.title: How the Four Elements Generate Matter

items.zh: 問：一切法生，皆從自種而起。云何說諸大種能生所造色耶？云何造色依彼，彼所建立，彼所任持，彼所長養耶？
items.en: Question: All dharmas arise from their own seed. How, then, can it be said that the great elements generate derived matter? And how is derived matter said to depend on them, to be established by them, to be sustained by them, and to be nourished by them?

items.zh: 答：由一切內外大種及所造色種子，皆悉依附內相續心。乃至諸大種子未生諸大以來，造色種子終不能生造色。
items.en: Answer: All the seeds of the great elements and of derived matter, whether internal or external, depend on the inwardly continuing mind. So long as the seeds of the great elements have not yet produced the great elements themselves, the seeds of derived matter can never produce derived matter.

items.zh: 要由彼生，造色方從自種子生，是故說彼能生造色，要由彼生為前導故。由此道理，說諸大種為彼生因。
items.en: Only once the great elements have arisen does derived matter then arise from its own seed. This is why it is said that the great elements generate derived matter: their arising must come first, as what leads the way. For this reason, the great elements are said to be the generating cause of derived matter.

items.zh: 云何造色依於彼耶？由造色生已，不離大種處而轉故。
items.en: How is derived matter said to depend on the great elements? Because once derived matter has arisen, it does not occur apart from the place occupied by the great elements.

items.zh: 云何彼所建立？由大種損益，彼同安危故。云何彼所任持？由隨大種等量不壞故。
items.en: How are the great elements said to establish derived matter? Because whenever the great elements are diminished or enhanced, derived matter shares the very same fortune, whether harm or safety. How are the great elements said to sustain derived matter? Because derived matter follows the exact measure of the great elements, remaining undiminished as long as they do.

items.zh: 云何彼所長養？由因飲食、睡眠、修習梵行三摩地等，依彼造色倍復增廣，故說大種為彼養因。如是諸大種望所造色有五種作用應知。
items.en: How are the great elements said to nourish derived matter? Because through food, sleep, the cultivation of pure conduct, meditative absorption, and the like, derived matter that depends on the great elements grows and expands all the more. This is why the great elements are said to be the nourishing cause of derived matter. Thus it should be understood that the great elements have five kinds of function towards the derived matter that depends on them.

items.zh: 復次，於色聚中、曾無極微生。若從自種生時，唯聚集生，或細或中或大。
items.en: Further, within a matter aggregate, no particle has ever, strictly speaking, arisen on its own. When matter arises from its own seed, it arises only as an aggregate, all at once — whether fine, middling, or coarse.

items.zh: 又非極微集成色聚。但由覺慧分析諸色極量邊際，分別假立以為極微。
items.en: Nor is a matter aggregate built up out of particles. Rather, it is only through discerning wisdom analysing matter down to its very outermost limit that a "particle" is conceptually distinguished and provisionally established.

items.title: Particles Have Location, But Not Parts

items.zh: 又色聚亦有方分，極微亦有方分，然色聚有分非極微。
items.en: Further, a matter aggregate has spatial location, and so does a particle. But a matter aggregate has further parts; a particle does not.

items.zh: 何以故？由極微即是分，此是聚色所有，非極微復有餘極微，是故極微非有分。
items.en: Why is this? Because the particle itself already is the part — the part that belongs to a matter aggregate — and a particle does not, in turn, contain some further particle within it. This is why a particle is said to have no further parts.

items.zh: 又不相離有二種。

items.title: Matter and Its Elements Never Separate

items.zh: 一、同處不相離。謂大種極微與色香味觸等，於無根處有離根者，於有根處有有根者，是名同處不相離。
items.en: First, non-separation in the same place: this means that the particles of the great elements, together with visible form, smell, taste, and the tangible, occur — in a place without sense-faculties, as particles apart from any faculty; in a place with sense-faculties, as particles belonging to a faculty. This is called non-separation in the same place.

items.zh: 二、和雜不相離。謂即此大種極微與餘聚集，能造、所造色處俱故，是名和雜不相離。
items.en: Second, non-separation through commingling: this means that these very particles of the great elements, together with other aggregated particles, occupy the very same place at once — the generating together with the generated matter. This is called non-separation through commingling.

items.zh: 又此遍滿聚色，應知如種種物，石磨為末，以水和合，互不相離；非如胡麻、綠豆、粟、稗等聚。
items.en: Further, it should be understood that this thoroughly pervading matter aggregate is like various substances ground by a millstone into powder and then mixed with water, mutually inseparable — not like a heap of sesame, mung beans, millet, and unhusked grain.

items.zh: 又一切所造色皆即依止大種處，不過大種處量；乃至大種所據處所，諸所造色還即據此；由此因緣，說所造色依於大種。即以此義，說諸大種名為大種。由此大種其性大故，為種生故。
items.en: Further, all derived matter depends entirely on the place occupied by the great elements and does not exceed the measure of that place; wherever the great elements occupy a place, derived matter occupies that very same place. For this reason it is said that derived matter depends on the great elements. It is by this very meaning that the great elements are called "great elements": because their nature is vast, and because they serve as the seed for what is generated.

items.zh: 復次，於諸色聚中，略有十四種事。謂地、水、火、風、色、聲、香、味、觸，及眼等五根。除唯意所行色。
items.en: Further, within matter aggregates in general, there are, in brief, fourteen categories of thing: earth, water, fire, wind; visible form, sound, smell, taste, the tangible; and the five faculties beginning with the eye. This excludes matter cognized by the mind-consciousness alone.

items.zh: 一切色聚，有色諸根所攝者，有一切，如所說事界。如有色諸根所攝聚如是，有色諸根所依大種所攝聚亦爾。所餘色聚，除有色諸根，唯有餘界。
items.en: Every matter aggregate belonging to a physical sense-faculty comprises all fourteen, in the sense of the causal elements already explained. Just as this holds for the aggregate belonging to a physical sense-faculty, so too it holds for the aggregate of the great elements on which a physical sense-faculty depends. As for the remaining matter aggregates — apart from the physical sense-faculties themselves — they comprise only the remaining elements.

items.title: Three Ways to Count What's There

items.zh: 又約相攝有十四事，即由相攝施設事極微。
items.en: Further, counted by distinguishing mark, there are fourteen categories; and it is by this same distinguishing mark that "particles" of each category are conceptually posited.

items.zh: 若約界攝，隨於此聚有爾所界，即說此聚爾所事攝。
items.en: Counted by causal element, however many elements are present within a given aggregate, that many categories are said to be comprised within that aggregate.

items.zh: 若約不相離攝，或內、或外所有諸聚。隨於此聚中，乃至有爾所法相可得，即說此聚爾所事攝應知。
items.en: Counted by non-separation — whether of an internal or an external aggregate — however many distinguishing marks can actually be found within a given aggregate, that many categories are said to be comprised within it; this should be understood accordingly.

items.zh: 所以者何？

items.title: How Many Elements Show Up in a Given Thing

items.zh: 或有聚中唯一大種可得。如石、末尼、真珠、琉璃、珂貝、璧玉、珊瑚等中，或池、沼、溝、渠、江、河等中，或火焰、燈燭等中，或四方風輪有塵、無塵風等中，
items.en: In some aggregates, only a single great element can be detected — as in stone, gems, pearls, lapis lazuli, coral, and the like; or in ponds, marshes, ditches, canals, and rivers; or in flame and lamplight; or in the winds of the four quarters, whether dust-bearing or dust-free.

items.zh: 或有聚中，二大種可得。如雪、濕樹、葉、花、果等中，或熱末尼等中。或有聚中三大種可得。如即熱樹等中，或動搖中。
items.en: In some aggregates, two great elements can be detected — as in snow, a moist tree, leaf, flower, or fruit, or in a heated gem. In some aggregates, three great elements can be detected — as in a tree that has caught fire, or in something being shaken by wind.

items.zh: 或有聚中四大種可得。謂於內色聚中。如薄伽梵說：於各別內身、若髮毛等乃至糞穢，是內地界；若小便等，是內水界；若於身中所有煖等，是內火界；若上行等風，是內風界。
items.en: In some aggregates, all four great elements can be detected — namely, within the aggregates that make up an internal, living body. As the Blessed One said: within each individual body, hair, body-hair, and the rest, down to excrement, are the internal earth element; urine and the like are the internal water element; whatever warmth is present within the body is the internal fire element; the upwards-moving and other winds are the internal wind element.

items.zh: 如是若於此聚彼相可得，說彼相為有；若不可得，說彼相為無。
items.en: Thus, whenever a given mark can be detected within an aggregate, that mark is said to be present; whenever it cannot be detected, it is said to be absent.

blocks.text: Fascicle 3 completes the Mind Stage. Having described the mind's five aspects and its seventeen powers, the treatise now steps back and classifies everything it has discussed. Today's reading is a short treatise on matter: how the four great elements relate to the matter derived from them, and whether matter is made of indivisible atoms. The Yogācāra answer is subtle and important, because it shows how the school can speak realistically about matter while holding that all things arise from seeds in consciousness.
Two tiny phrases are untranslated: 0290a23 "inseparability, further, is of two kinds" and 0290b16 "why is this?".

All five aspects discussed so far (self-nature, support, object, accompaniments, activity) fall into three categories: **matter aggregates** (色聚), **mind and mental factors** (心心所), and **the unconditioned** (無為). "This excludes all other conceptually existent dharmas."

Both teachers say what is excluded: the twenty-four **formations dissociated from mind**, such as time, direction, sequence, and speed, which we met on Day 1. Venerable Miào Jìng: they "have no substance of their own, so they are not counted"; they are labels set up on the configuration of matter and mind. The five classes of the *Hundred Dharmas* thus shrink to three real ones here.

subs.head: How can elements "generate" matter if everything comes from seeds?

blocks.text: A good question, raised by the treatise itself. Every dharma arises from its own seed, so how can the four **great elements** (大種, *mahābhūta*) "generate" **derived matter** (造色, *upādāya-rūpa*)? The answer: all seeds, inner and outer, depend on the continuing mind (the ālayavijñāna). The seeds of derived matter cannot produce their result until the great elements have arisen. The elements "lead the way", and in that sense they generate.

Venerable Miào Jìng places this precisely among the four conditions (Day 1): the great elements are only the **dominant condition**; "the causal condition is still the seed in the ālayavijñāna." This is how Yogācāra keeps ordinary physics without giving matter independent reality.

Towards derived matter the great elements have five functions: they **generate** it (lead the way), **support** it (it never occurs apart from their place), **establish** it (it shares their fortune, harm or safety), **sustain** it (it follows their measure), and **nourish** it (food, sleep, pure conduct, and meditation make it grow). The word "establish" echoes Day 6, where body and mind were said to share "one fate".

"Within a matter aggregate, no particle has ever, strictly speaking, arisen on its own." Matter arises from its seed only as an aggregate (色聚). A **particle** (極微, *paramāṇu*) is "conceptually distinguished" when discerning wisdom analyses matter to its outermost limit. Nor is an aggregate built up from particles.

This reverses the atomism of the Sarvāstivāda and Vaiśeṣika schools, for whom real atoms are the building blocks. For Yogācāra, the atom is a limit of analysis, a concept, not a constituent. Master Cháng Bǎi's image, from Ru-Yi's reading note: a dewdrop in the sun does not shrink to a final smallest droplet before vanishing; it simply dries away. Decrease of matter was never a peeling-off of real atoms.
The treatise adds a fine distinction. Both an aggregate and a particle have location (方分), but an aggregate has parts and a particle does not, because the particle already *is* a part.

The elements and derived matter are inseparable in two ways: in the same place, and by **commingling**, "like various substances ground by a millstone into powder and mixed with water", unlike a heap of sesame and beans that can be sorted again. Why are they called "great elements"? Because their nature is vast, and because they are the "seed" (種) for what they generate, in the sense that they must come first.

Matter aggregates comprise fourteen things: the four elements; the five sense objects (visible form, sound, smell, taste, the tangible); and the five sense faculties. This "excludes matter cognized by the mind alone", which Venerable Miào Jìng identifies as the form of the sphere of dharmas: the "form" of precepts, its absence, and form produced in meditation. The "form" of precepts, he says, is really a firm inner resolve, "I will keep the precepts".

subs.head: How many elements in a given thing?

blocks.text: In some aggregates only earth can be detected, in others two, three, or all four: a burning tree shows earth, water (moisture), and fire. The detail matters less than the principle behind it, which Day 17 states outright: all four are always present as causes, even when only some are manifest.

quiz.q: Fascicle 3 opens by saying the five things discussed so far — self-nature through activity — are all comprised within three categories. What are they?
options: the desire, form, and formless realms
matter aggregates, mind and mental factors, and the unconditioned
wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate
faculty, object, and consciousness
quiz.why: "Namely: the category of matter aggregates, the category of mind and mental factors, and the category of unconditioned dharmas." Venerable Miào Jìng: Yogācāra sorts all dharmas into five classes — form, mind, mental factors, dissociated forces, and the unconditioned — and the three categories take four of them, because "this excludes all other conceptually existent dharmas." A, C, and D are classifications used elsewhere.

quiz.q: After the three categories the text adds, "This excludes all other conceptually existent dharmas." What do both teachers say is excluded, and why?
options: the unconditioned, because it neither arises nor ceases
the five faculties, because they are invisible
the mental factors, because they depend on mind
the twenty-four forces dissociated from mind (time, direction, flux, swiftness, and the like) — they have no substance of their own, only labels set up on the configuration of matter and mind
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: "Conceptually existent dharmas have no substance of their own, so they are not counted … things like 'time, direction, flux, swiftness' … twenty-four dissociated factors in all, all conceptually existent." Master Cháng Bǎi likewise says they are not separately real entities, only convenient labels for the configuration of matter and mind that already exists. §62 lists all twenty-four. A and C are inside the three categories.

quiz.q: All dharmas arise from their own seeds, yet the treatise says the great elements "generate" derived matter. According to Venerable Miào Jìng, which of the four conditions is the great elements' role as "generating cause"?
options: the causal condition
the condition of immediate succession
the object-condition
the dominant condition — the true causal condition is still derived matter's own seed in the ālayavijñāna
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: "Among the four conditions it should be the dominant condition; it cannot count as the causal condition — the causal condition is still the seed in the ālayavijñāna." The text's point is that the elements must arise first, "as what leads the way," and only then does derived matter arise from its own seed. Master Cháng Bǎi draws the same line: derived matter's seed is the real producing cause; the elements are an indispensable lead condition. A is exactly the misunderstanding to avoid.

quiz.q: According to the treatise, how many functions do the great elements have towards the derived matter that depends on them?
options: three: arising, abiding, ceasing
five: generating, supporting, establishing, sustaining, and nourishing
four: hardness, moisture, warmth, motion
one: generating
quiz.why: "Thus it should be understood that the great elements have five kinds of function towards the derived matter that depends on them": generating (leading the way), supporting (it never occurs apart from their place), establishing (sharing their fortune), sustaining (following their measure), and nourishing (growing through food and the like). Venerable Miào Jìng sums up: "generating, supporting, establishing, sustaining, nourishing — these five causes." C lists the elements' own qualities, not their functions towards derived matter.

quiz.q: What is the treatise's position on "particles"?
options: no particle has ever arisen on its own; matter arises from its seed only as an aggregate, and a "particle" is provisionally posited where analysis reaches matter's outermost limit
particles are real ultimate units, and aggregates are built up from them
particles exist only in the form realm
particles were created by Mahābrahmā
quiz.why: "Within a matter aggregate, no particle has ever, strictly speaking, arisen on its own … Nor is a matter aggregate built up out of particles. Rather, it is only through discerning wisdom analysing matter down to its very outermost limit that a 'particle' is conceptually distinguished and provisionally established." B is the view of other schools the treatise rejects. Venerable Miào Jìng: aggregates arise "all at once," "not first a particle and then gradually more"; the name "particle" "is set up by people's discriminating mind."

quiz.q: What image does the treatise use for the great elements and derived matter being "inseparable through commingling"?
options: like a heap of sesame, mung beans, millet, and grain
like various substances ground by a millstone into powder and mixed with water, mutually inseparable
like oil floating on water
like a shadow following a body
quiz.why: "Like various substances ground by a millstone into powder and then mixed with water, mutually inseparable — not like a heap of sesame, mung beans, millet, and unhusked grain." A is the explicit contrast — mixed but easily separated again. Venerable Miào Jìng gives apples, oranges, and bananas ground and mixed with water; Master Cháng Bǎi uses flour kneaded into dough, noting that some Śrāvaka schools hold the elements merely sit side by side, while the Mahāyāna position is that they genuinely fuse.

quiz.q: The treatise says matter aggregates comprise, in brief, fourteen kinds of thing. What are they?
options: the eighteen elements minus four
the five aggregates, six faculties, and three realms
earth, water, fire, wind; visible form, sound, smell, taste, the tangible; and the five faculties beginning with the eye — excluding matter cognized by the mind alone
the twelve sense-fields plus two unconditioned
quiz.why: "Earth, water, fire, wind; visible form, sound, smell, taste, the tangible; and the five faculties beginning with the eye. This excludes matter cognized by the mind-consciousness alone." Venerable Miào Jìng: four plus five plus five makes fourteen. The excluded "matter cognized by the mind alone" is form comprised in the sphere of dharmas (see Q3-2).
